Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 37, verses 1–5:

Meccan, and it has one hundred and eighty-one verses. It is also said to have eighty-two, and that it was revealed after al-An'am. In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Allah, glorified is He, swears by groups of angels, or by their souls, ﴿those who stand in ranks﴾, either their feet standing in prayer, from His saying ﴿and indeed We are those who stand in ranks﴾, or their wings in the air, standing and awaiting the command of Allah. ﴿Then those who drive﴾ the clouds, driving them. ﴿Then those who recite﴾ the words of Allah from the revealed books and others. It has been said that ﴿those who stand in ranks﴾ are the birds, from His saying ﴿and the birds in ranks﴾. ﴿Those who drive﴾ is everything that drives away from the disobedience of Allah. ﴿Those who recite﴾ is everyone who recites the Book of Allah.

It is also permissible that He swears by the souls of the scholars who act, who stand in ranks in tahajjud (night prayer) and the other prayers and in the rows of congregation. ﴿Those who drive﴾ are those who drive with admonitions and advice. ﴿Those who recite﴾ are the verses of Allah, and ﴿those who study﴾ are His laws. Or He swears by the souls of the commanders of those who fight in the way of Allah, which arrange the battle rows, drive the horses for jihad, and recite the remembrance [Mahmud said: "The one sworn by is groups of angels or their souls, and what is meant is their arranging themselves in prayer, their driving of the clouds, that is their driving them, and their reciting the remembrance of Allah; or the scholars, and what is meant is their feet being arranged in prayer, their driving away from sins with admonitions, and their reciting the remembrance..." up to his saying: "And the differentiation between the groups may be either that the first is the best, or the reverse." Ahmad said: It has been permitted that their order in precedence is that the first is the best, and the reverse. He did not explain the basis of each of them from the standpoint of the art of al-badi' (rhetorical embellishment). We explain it, so we say: the reason for beginning with the best is attention to what is most important, so it is put first. The reason for the reverse of this is ascent from the lower to the higher, and from it is his saying:

"Among them by night was Ja'far, and the son of his mother,
'Ali; and among them was Ahmad al-Munakhkhir."

It should not be said that this was permitted only because the waw (and) does not imply rank. Its utmost is that it is an excuse. What we have mentioned is a statement of what it contains of the requirements of al-badi' and eloquence. In this verse there is evidence for the position of Sibawayh and al-Khalil regarding such as ﴿by the night when it covers﴾ and ﴿by the day when it displays itself﴾: they say that the second waw and what follows it are conjunctive. Others hold that they are particles of oath. So the occurrence of the fa' (then) in this verse in the place of the waw has the same meaning, except that what the fa' adds of ordering is clear evidence that the waw occurring in such a context is for conjunction, not for oath.] Along with that, those preoccupations do not distract them from Him, as is related of 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him.

If you ask: what is the rule of the fa' when it comes as a conjunction between attributes? I say: either it indicates the sequence of their meanings in existence, as in the line:

"Alas for Zayyaba, for al-Harith the dawn-raider,
then the plunderer, then the returner."

It is as if it were said: the one who raided at dawn, then plundered, then returned. Or it indicates the sequence of them in degree of excellence in some respects, as when you say: take the better, then the best, and do the good, then the finer. Or it indicates the sequence of their subjects in that respect, as in his saying: "May Allah have mercy on those who shave, then those who trim." On these three principles the function of the conjunctive fa' in attributes is governed.

If you ask: on which of these principles is it in what you are dealing with? I say: if you unify the subject, it indicates the sequence of the attributes in excellence; and if you make it three, it indicates the sequence of the subjects in it. The explanation: when you apply these attributes to the angels and make them comprehensive of them, then joining them with fa' implies a sequence of them in excellence: either the excellence is for the arranging, then the driving, then the reciting, or the reverse. Likewise if you mean the scholars and the commanders of the raiders. If you apply the first attribute to one group and the second and third to other groups, then it indicates the sequence of the subjects in excellence, meaning that the groups of those who stand in ranks have merit, those who drive have more merit, and those who recite have greater merit still; or the reverse. Likewise if you mean by those who stand in ranks: the birds; by those who drive: everything that drives away from disobedience; and by those who recite: every soul that recites the remembrance, for the subjects are then different.

It has been read with the assimilation of the ta' into the sad, the zay, and the dhal. ﴿Lord of the heavens and the earth﴾ is a predicate after a predicate, or a predicate of an omitted subject. ﴿The easts﴾: there are three hundred and sixty easts, and likewise the wests. The sun rises each day in one of its easts and sets in one of its wests, and it does not rise or set in the same one on two days.

If you ask: what did He mean by His saying ﴿Lord of the two easts and Lord of the two wests﴾? I say: He meant the easts and wests of summer and winter.

Al-dunya al-qurba minkum: the nearest heaven to you. And "al-zina" (adornment) is a verbal noun, like "al-nisba," and also a noun for that with which a thing is adorned, just as "al-liqa" is the noun for that with which the inkwell is wiped (or smeared). Both meanings are possible in His words, ﴿with an adornment, the stars﴾. If you take it as the verbal noun, then it is an idafa (genitive construction) to the agent, meaning: that the stars adorned it; its original form being "bi-zinatin al-kawakib." Or it is an idafa to the object, meaning: that God adorned the stars and made them beautiful, since they adorned the sky only through their own beauty; its original form being "bi-zinatin al-kawakib." This is the reading of Abu Bakr, al-A'mash and Ibn Thab. If you take it as the noun, the idafa has two possibilities:

First, that "the stars" be an explanation (bayan) of the adornment, because the adornment is vague as to the stars and other things with which something may be adorned. Second, that it means what the stars were adorned with. It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, that "bi-zinatin al-kawakib" means "with the light of the stars." It is also permissible that it means their various shapes, such as the shape of the Pleiades (al-Thurayya), the Great Bear (Banat Na'sh), Orion (al-Jawza'), and others, and their risings and their settings. It has also been read with this meaning, "bi-zinatin al-kawakib," with the word "zina" tanwin-ed and "al-kawakib" in the genitive as a substitution (badal). In the case of the accusative of "al-kawakib," it may be a substitution for the position (mahall) of "bi-zinatin," as occurs according to the sense, because the meaning is: We created the stars as an adornment for the heaven and as a protection from the devils, as He, Exalted, said: ﴿And We have certainly adorned the nearest heaven with lamps, and made them missiles against the devils﴾. It is also permissible to supply the causal verb, as if it were said: "and as a protection from every devil, We adorned it with the stars," or it was said: "and We protected it with protection." And "al-marid" is:

The evidence for this is His saying after enumerating these things: ﴿So ask them: are they harder to create, or those whom We have created?﴾ with the *fa'* of consequence. His saying ﴿or those whom We have created﴾ is unrestricted, without specification by explanation, relying on the explanation of what precedes it, as if He said: We created such-and-such wonders and marvels of creation, so ask them whether they are harder to create or those that We have created from these things. This is confirmed by the recitation (*qira'ah*) of those who read *am man 'addadna* (or those whom We counted), with lightening and with doubling.

﴿Harder to create﴾ may mean stronger in creation, from the saying "severe in creation," and "there is severity in his creation," and more difficult and more laborious, in the sense of a rebuttal of their denial of resurrection and of the second creation. Whoever finds the creation of these great creatures easy, and for whom their invention was not difficult, the creation of humans is easier for him. ﴿And He created them from clay that sticks﴾ is either a testimony against them of weakness and flaccidity, since what is made from clay is not described as hard and strong, or an argument against them, that the clay that sticks from which they were created is dust, so why do they deny being created from dust like it, when they said: ﴿When we are dust, shall we...?﴾ This meaning is supported by what follows of their denial of resurrection. It was said: "those whom We have created" refers to the past nations, but this view is not suitable.

It is recited *lazib* and *latib*, and the meaning is one. *Ath-thaqib* means the very bright.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 37, verse 12–14:

Rather, you (O Muhammad) marvel at the power of God over these great creations, while they mock you, your marvelling, and what you show them of the signs of God's power. Or (the verse means): you marvel at their denial of resurrection, while they mock the matter of resurrection.

It is also recited with a dammah on the ta' (ʿajibtu, "I marvel"), meaning: the greatness of My signs and the abundance of My creatures has reached the point that I Myself marvel at them. How much more so for My servants? Yet these people, out of their ignorance and obstinacy, mock My signs. Or (the meaning is): I marvel that they deny resurrection, coming from One whose acts are these, while they mock one who describes God as being able to do it.

If you ask: how is marvelling permissible for God, Exalted is He, when it is only an awe that overtakes a human being upon regarding something as great, and awe is not permissible for God? I answer: there are two aspects to this. The first: marvelling is stripped of its meaning and taken to mean regarding something as great. The second: marvelling is imagined and supposed.

It has also come in a hadith: "Your Lord marvels at your despair (qunut) and your quickness in answering you" [[The phrase "from your al-ʾall and your despair": al-ʾall comes in the sense of haste, moaning and corruption, as stated in al-Sihah. (ʿ)]] [[Abu ʿUbayd related it in Gharib al-hadith from Muhammad ibn ʿAmr, raising it (to the Prophet). Then he said: al-ʾall is raising the voice in supplication. Some of them said: it is narrated as al-awwal, which means hardship.]]. Shurayh used to recite it with a fathah and say: "Indeed God does not marvel at anything; He marvels only at one who does not know." Ibrahim al-Nakhaʿi said: "Shurayh was pleased with his own knowledge, while ʿAbdullah is more knowledgeable," meaning ʿAbdullah ibn Masʿud, who used to recite it with a dammah.

It was also said that its meaning is: "Say, O Muhammad, 'Rather, I marvel.'"

And when they are reminded, their habit is that when they are admonished with something, they do not take heed of it; and when they see a sign from the signs of God, clear as the splitting of the moon or the like, they exaggerate in mockery (yastasKHirūn). Or some of them urge others to mock it.

Wa-ābā'unā is conjoined either to the place (maḥall) of inna and its noun, or to the pronoun in mab'ūthūn, and the conjunction was permitted with that pronoun because of the separation by the interrogative hamza. The meaning is: "Will our fathers too be raised?" with added emphasis on the improbability, they meaning that the fathers are older, so their being raised is even more remote and more absurd.

It is read as "aw ābā'unā" (or our fathers), and "qul naʿam" (say: yes), and "naʿam" with the ʿayn vowelled with a kasra, and both are dialectal forms. It is also read "qāla naʿam," that is, God Most High or the Messenger (ﷺ) said it. The meaning is: "Yes, you will be raised, while you are ṣāghirūn (humbled, abased)."

Fa-innamā is the answer to a suppressed condition, whose implied sense is: "If that is so, then it is only one shout (zajrah wāḥidah), and it does not return to anything; rather it is an ambiguous term whose clarification is its predicate." It is permissible to read it as:

"Fa-innamā al-baʿthah zajrah wāḥidah," meaning: the raising is one shout, and it is the second blast (al-nafkhah al-thāniyah).

Al-zajrah (the shout) is from your saying: "zajara al-rāʿī al-ibil aw al-ghanam," when the herdsman shouts at the camels or the sheep, so they are startled by his voice. From it is the line of poetry:

*Zajra Abī ʿUrwah al-sibāʿa idhā*
*Ashfaqa an yakhtalaṭna bil-ghanam*

[[This is from al-Nābighah al-Ja'dī. Abū ʿUrwah is the kunyah of al-ʿAbbās, the uncle of the Prophet (ﷺ). They used to claim that he would shout at the predators so that the bile of the lion would burst in its belly. It is related that a raid came upon them on the day of Ḥunayn, and he shouted: "Yā ṣabāḥāh!" and pregnant women miscarried, and his voice could be heard from a distance of eight miles. His "zajara yazjuru" means when he shouts to prevent it; that is: like the shout of Abū ʿUrwah at the predators away from the sheep when he fears their mixing with them in the desert.]]

He intends its being a call by which they are summoned. Then: *fa-idhā hum aḥyā'un baṣīrūn yanẓurūn* ("then, behold, they will be alive, seeing, looking").

This may be that the words "this is the Day of Religion" up to His saying "gather them" are spoken by the disbelievers to one another, and that they may be spoken by the angels to them. And it may be that "Woe to us! This is the Day of Religion" is the speech of the disbelievers, and "This is the Day of Decision" is the speech of the angels, answering them. "The Day of Religion" (yawm al-din): the day on which we are repaid (nadin), that is, we are recompensed for our deeds. "The Day of Decision" (yawm al-fasl): the day of judgment, and the separating between the groups of guidance and error.

"Gather together" — God's address to the angels, or one of them addressing another. "And their spouses (azwajahum) and what they used to worship" — transmitted from the Prophet ﷺ: their counterparts and peers among the sinners, the people of fornication with the people of fornication, and the people of theft with the people of theft. It was also said: their companion devils. And it was said: their wives who share their religion. "And guide them" — make them aware of the path to the Fire so that they may enter it. This is mockery of them and a rebuke, pointing to their inability to help one another, after they had been, in the world, mutually supportive and helpful. "Rather, today they are submitting" — some of them have surrendered to others and abandoned them out of helplessness, so all of them are submitting, none of them victorious. It has been read as "la tatanasarun" and "la tanasarun," with assimilation (idgham).

The right side was the more honoured and stronger of the two limbs, and they would attribute blessing to it. With it they shake hands, wipe, give and receive, and carry out most affairs. They regard the left as ill omen, and for this reason they called it the "unlucky one" (al-shu'ma), just as they called its counterpart the "right one" (al-yumna). They took omens from the sanih (a gazelle or bird passing from left to right) and took ill omen from the barih (passing from right to left). The left-handed person was disliked among them. The Sacred Law (al-shari'a) confirmed this, so it commanded that noble matters be undertaken with the right hand and base matters with the left. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) loved to start from the right in everything. [[Agreed upon (muttafaq 'alayh), from the hadith of 'A'isha (may God be pleased with her), and more complete than this.]] The right hand was assigned to the recorder of good deeds and the left to the recorder of evil deeds. The doer of good was promised that his record would be given to him in his right hand, and the wrongdoer that it would be given to him in his left.

The phrase is borrowed for the direction and side of good, so it is said: "He came to him from the right," meaning from the direction and side of good. He thus turned him away from it and led him astray. It is mentioned in some tafsirs: whoever the Devil comes to from the right, he comes to him from the direction of religion and confuses the truth for him. Whoever he comes to from the left, he comes to him from the direction of desires. Whoever he comes to from in front, he comes to him through denial of the Resurrection, of reward and of punishment. Whoever he comes to from behind, he frightens him with poverty for himself and for those who will succeed him, so he does not maintain kinship ties and does not pay zakat.

If you say: their saying "he came to him from the side and direction of good" is itself a metaphor, so how have you made "the right" a metaphor of a metaphor? I say: among metaphors is that which has become dominant in usage until it has joined the literal meanings, and this is of that kind. You may also make it a borrowing for strength and domination, because the right hand is described as strong and by it force is exercised. The meaning is: you used to come to us by strength and domination, and approach us by authority and might, until you compelled us to error and forced us into it. This is the speech of followers to their leaders, and of the misguided to their devils.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 37, verses 40–49:

﴿Except the sincere servants of Allah﴾. The exception here is disconnected (istithna' munqati', an exception whose excluded item is not of the same category as what precedes it). He explains "the known provision" (al-rizq al-ma'lum) as fruits.

Fruit is everything that is enjoyed for pleasure and not eaten to sustain health. The meaning is that all their provision is fruit, because they are free of the need to preserve their health through staple foods. They are bodies that are firmly made and created for eternity, so everything they eat, they eat for enjoyment. It is also permissible to mean: a known provision described by the qualities it was created with: good taste, fragrance, delight, and beautiful appearance. It has also been said: "known" in terms of its time, as in His saying, ﴿And they will have their provision therein, morning and evening﴾. It is also reported from Qatadah that "the known provision" is Paradise. His saying, ﴿in gardens﴾, rejects this. His saying, ﴿and they will be honoured﴾, is what the scholars say in defining reward, in praise and glorification. It is among the greatest things that souls of high resolve should long for, just as among the greatest things from which their souls should recoil is the state of the people of the Fire and their young.

"Facing one another" (al-tuqabul): this is more complete for joy and more intimate. It has also been said: none of them looks at the back of another's neck.

The cup containing wine is called "ka's" (cup), and wine itself is called ka's. He said:

*"And many a cup I drank for pleasure,*
*and another I drank to cure the first with it,*
*so that people may know that I am a man*
*who has come at life through its door."*

This is by al-A'sha. The ka's is applied to the glass containing wine, and to the wine within it, as a well-known metonymy. It is feminine, as shown by the feminine form of its adjective and pronoun. He says: many a cup I drank with delight, or for the sake of delight, which harmed me, so I drank another cup to cure the first with it, so that people may know that I am experienced in affairs. He alluded to this by his saying, "I have come at life through its door." **Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 37, verses 50–57:**

If you ask: "On what is His saying ﴿So they will turn to one another, questioning﴾ conjoined?" I answer: it is conjoined to ﴿they will be served﴾ (yuṭāfu ʿalayhim). The meaning is: they drink, and they converse over the wine, in the customary way of drinking. [[His words "in the customary way of drinking" (ka-ʿādat al-shurb): the plural of shārib (drinker), like ṣaḥb as the plural of ṣāḥib (companion), as stated in al-Ṣiḥāḥ (the lexicon of al-Jawharī). (ʿ)]] He said:

*"Nothing of pleasures remains except the talk of the noble over wine."* [[This is by al-Farazdaq. He means: no pleasure of the pleasures remains except the pleasure of the talk of the noble, or: no desirable appetite of the delightful appetites remains except the talk of the noble over wine. He used the preposition ʿalā (over), because the drink is before them while the talk comes from their mouths, above it. The expected wording would be "wa-mā baqiya min al-ladhdhāt", but he made the verb feminine because it is governed by the restrictive "illā" (except), or on the earlier interpretation.]]

So ﴿they will turn to one another, questioning﴾ means they will question one another about what happened to them and against them in the world. Yet it is expressed in the past tense, in keeping with God's way in reporting [such matters].

It is read ﴿among the believers﴾ (al-muṣaddiqīn), from taṣdīq (affirming). It is also read ﴿among the almsgivers﴾ (al-muṣṣaddiqīn), with the ṣād doubled, from taṣaddaq (giving alms). It is said that this was revealed concerning a man who gave his wealth in charity for the sake of God, then fell into need and asked one of his brothers for help. He said: "Where is your wealth?" He said: "I gave it in charity, so that God would compensate me with something better than it in the Hereafter." So he said:

﴿Are you among those who affirm the Day of Judgment?﴾ Or [it means] "among those who give alms seeking reward." "By God, I will not give you anything."

﴿Shall we indeed be recompensed?﴾ That is, shall we be requited, from dīn, which means recompense. Or: shall we be governed and ordered? It is said: "dānahu sāsahu" (he governed him).

From this comes the hadith: *"The intelligent person is one who holds himself accountable"* [[Related by al-Tirmidhī and Ibn Mājah, al-Ḥākim, Aḥmad, al-Bazzār, Abū Yaʿlā, al-Ḥārith and al-Ṭabarānī, all through the narration of Abū Bakr ibn Abī Maryam, from Ḍamrah ibn Ḥabīb, from Shaddād ibn Aws.]]

He said, meaning that speaker: ﴿Would you like to look down?﴾ ﴿and He will look down and see him in the midst of the Fire﴾ — [i.e.,] "Would you like to look down into the Fire, so that I may show you that companion?" It has been said that in Paradise there are openings through which its people look at the people of the Fire. And it has been said that the speaker is God, Mighty and Majestic. It has also been said that some of the angels say to the people of Paradise: "Would you like to look down, so that you may know where your station is compared with the station of the people of the Fire?"

It is also read ﴿would you look down?﴾ (muṭṭaliʿūn, fa-aṭṭaliʿ), with the verb in the past form and in the present subjunctive. And [it is read] ﴿fa-aṭṭalaʿa﴾ with tashdīd (doubling), following the form of the past and the subjunctive present: "muṭṭaliʿūna fa-aṭṭalaʿa." And ﴿fa-aṭlaʿa﴾ with takhfīf (no doubling), following the form of the past and the subjunctive present. It is said: "ṭalaʿa ʿalaynā fulān," "iṭṭalaʿa," and "aṭlaʿa," with one meaning. The meaning is: "Would you look down upon the companion, so that I too may look down?" Or: looking down was offered to them, and they declined it, and then he looked down himself.

If you take iṭṭilāʿ (looking down) as from aṭlaʿahu ghayruhu (another made him look), the meaning is: he made his looking down conditional upon their looking down, and this is one of the manners of companionship, that one should not act independently of his companions in anything, so they are as if they were looking down with him. It has been said that on this reading the address is to the angels.

It is also read ﴿muṭṭaliʿūnī﴾ with the nūn kasrah, meaning "muṭṭaliʿūnī" (looking down at me), where the attached pronoun is placed in the position of the detached one, as in his saying:

*"They are the doers of good and the ones who command it, when they fear some great calamity of time."* [[Here al-khayr (the good) is in the accusative as the object. One says "amartuka al-khayr" and "amartuka bihi." So al-āmirūnahu is an active participle transitive to its second object directly. Its proper form should have been separated, but it was joined, and perhaps the line is more forceful than the bare active participle without lām. The mā is superfluous: i.e., when they fear some grave matter of time. In another version it reads "mufẓiʿan" (dreadful), meaning frightening, so it belongs in the letter ʿayn.]]

Or the active participle in this sense is made like the present tense because of the affinity between them, as if he had said: "you look down." But this is weak and occurs only in poetry.

﴿In the midst of the Blazing Fire﴾: in its middle. One says "taʿibtu ḥattā inqaṭaʿa sawāʾī" (I grew weary until my middle was cut off). And on the authority of Abū ʿUbaydah: ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar said to me, "I was writing, O Abā ʿUbaydah, until my middle was cut off."

﴿Indeed (in) it almost led me astray﴾: in is the light (mukhaffafah) form of the heavy (thaqīlah) one, and it enters upon kāda (almost) as it enters upon kāna and the like. ﴿The favor of my Lord﴾ is the protection and success in holding fast to the handle of Islam, and in disavowal of an evil companion. Or it is God's bestowal of reward and of being among the people of Paradise.

﴿Among those brought forth﴾: among those who were brought to punishment, just as you and your like were brought.

The commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 37, verses 75-82:

When He mentioned the sending of warners to the earlier nations and the evil end of the warned, He followed this with the mention of Noah and his supplication to Him when he despaired of his people. The lam (emphatic lam) that enters upon ﴿نِعْمَ﴾ is the answer to an omitted oath, and the object of praise is omitted; its estimate is: "By God, indeed excellent are We as Answerers." The use of the plural signifies majesty and grandeur. The meaning is:

"We answered him in the best answer, and brought it to his desired aim and purpose: victory over his enemies and vengeance upon them in the most eloquent manner." ﴿وَجَعَلْنَا ذُرِّيَّتَهُ هُمُ الْبَاقِينَ﴾: "They are the ones who remained alone, while others perished." It is related that everyone who was with him in the ark died except his offspring. Or, "They are the ones whose descendants continued until the Day of Resurrection." Qatadah said: "All people are descendants of Noah." Noah, peace be upon him, had three sons: Sam, Ham, and Japheth (Yafith). Sam is the father of the Arabs, Persians (Faris), and Romans (Rum). Ham is the father of the black peoples from east to west. Japheth is the father of the Turks, Gog and Magog (Ya'juj and Ma'juj).

﴿وَتَرَكْنَا عَلَيْهِ فِي الْآخِرِينَ﴾ among the nations after him this statement: ﴿سَلَامٌ عَلَى نُوحٍ﴾, meaning: they greet him with peace, in a complete greeting, and they pray for him. It is from reported speech (al-kalam al-mahki), like your saying: "I read a surah which We sent down" (qara'tu suratan anzalnaha). 

If you ask: "What is the meaning of His saying ﴿فِي الْعَالَمِينَ﴾?" I say: its meaning is a supplication for the permanence of this salutation among all of them, and that no one among them be devoid of it. It is as if it were said: "God established the greeting upon Noah and perpetuated it among the angels and the two weighty ones (al-thaqalan, jinn and humankind), who greet him, all of them, without exception."

He explained the recompense of Noah, peace be upon him, with that noble honor, namely the preservation of his remembrance and the greeting of all worlds upon him until the end of time, by his being a doer of good. Then He explained his being a doer of good by his being a believing servant, to show you the greatness of the station of faith, that it is the utmost of the attributes of praise and exaltation, and to make you desire it and increase in it.

**Among his partisans** — that is, those who followed him in the fundamentals of religion, even though their revealed laws (sharai') differed. Between Noah and Abraham there were only two prophets: Hud and Salih. And between Noah and Abraham there were two thousand six hundred and forty years.

If you ask: To what does the adverbial phrase (al-zarf) attach?

I say: to what is contained in "al-shi'ah" of the meaning of "al-mushayaʿah" (following), meaning: and among those who followed him in his religion and his piety, when he came to his Lord with a sound heart (qalb salim). Or it is attached to an omitted element, which is: "Remember [when he came to his Lord] with a sound heart," sound from all the afflictions of hearts. It has also been said: sound from shirk. There is no point in restricting it, since it is unrestricted (mutlaq), so no affliction is preferred over another, and it encompasses all of them.

If you ask: What is the meaning of his coming to his Lord with his heart? I say: its meaning is that he sincerely devoted his heart to God, and this was known from him, so the coming was made an example (mathal) for that.

"Ifkan" (ﷻ إِفْكاً) is an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu), its estimated sense being: "Do you desire gods other than God as a falsehood?" in the stars: in the science of the stars (astrology), or in their book, or in their judgments. It is reported of some kings that he was asked about what he desired, and he said: "A beloved whom I look at, a needy one whom I look after, and a book in which I look." The people were astrologers (nejjamin, practitioners of astrology), and he gave them the impression that he had deduced from a sign in the science of the stars that he would fall ill. So ﴿He said: "Indeed, I am sick"﴾, meaning: I am about to become sick with the plague, and it was the most prevalent of the diseases among them. They feared contagion so that they would scatter away from him, so they fled from him to their festival and left him in the house of the idols with no one else with him, and he did to the idols what he did.

If you ask: how was it permissible for him to lie? I say: some people have permitted it in war stratagem, in taqiyya (precautionary dissimulation), in pleasing a spouse, and in reconciling those who are quarrelling or estranged. The sound view is that lying is forbidden except when one speaks by allusion and equivocation (tawriya). What Ibrahim (peace be upon him) said was a ma'rad (an equivocal statement), and he intended by it that whoever has death around his neck is sick.

From this is the proverb: "Safety is enough of an affliction." And the verse of Labid:

*"So I prayed to my Lord for safety, earnestly, that He might make me healthy; but then safety became an affliction."* [[*"My spear did not bend to one who pressed it, until the mornings and evenings softened it."*

It is by Labid ibn Rabi'a al-'Amiri. The qanah (spear) is the lance, which he used as a metaphor for his uprightness or his strength by way of explicit statement. Softness (al-layyuna) and pressing (al-ghamz) are a complement (tarshih). Al-ghamz is pressing with the hand. Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 37, verses 91–93:

﴿Then he turned to their gods﴾: he went to them secretly, from the "rawgha" of the fox (the sly sidelong move), to their gods, that is, to their idols which, in their claim, were gods. Compare His saying, ﴿Where are My partners?﴾ and ﴿Will you not eat? What is wrong with you that you do not speak?﴾, mocking them and their abasement below the state of their worshippers.

﴿Then he turned upon them﴾: he came upon them while concealing himself, as if he said: he struck them, a blow (ḍarban), because "rāgha ʿalayhim" carries the sense of "ḍarabahum" (he struck them). Or ﴿turned upon them, striking﴾ (yaḍribuhum ḍarban). Or ﴿turned upon them, striking﴾ with the meaning of "ḍāribān" (striking). It is also read ṣafqan and safqan, and both mean striking.

The meaning of ﴿striking with the right hand﴾ (ḍarban bil-yamīn) is a severe, powerful blow, because the right hand is the stronger and mightier of the two limbs. It was also said: "with strength and firmness." And it was said: "because of the oath," which is His saying, ﴿By God, I will surely scheme against your idols﴾.

**Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 37, verse 94:**

*Yaziffun* (يَزِفُّونَ): they hasten, from the *zafif* of the ostrich (the quick, gliding run of an ostrich). *Yazuffun* (ويزفون) comes from *azalla*, meaning he entered into *zafif*. Or it comes from *azaffahu*, meaning he made him run at *zafif*, so that some of them drive others on, that is, *yuzaffuba'duhum ba'dan* (some of them hasten others). *Yuzafun* (ويزفون), in the passive form, means they are driven to run at *zafif*. *Yazifun* (ويزفون) comes from *wazifa yazifu*, meaning he hastened. *Yuzafun* (ويزفون) comes from *zaffahu* when *hadahu* (he drove him on), so that some of them drive others on because of their eagerness towards him.

If you say: between this and the words of God Most High, "They said: Who has done this to our gods? Indeed he is among the wrongdoers. They said: We heard a youth mention them, called Abraham," there seems to be a contradiction. Here it is mentioned that they turned away from him out of fear of contagion, but when they saw him breaking them, they came towards him rushing to restrain him and to lay hands on him. Then it is mentioned that they asked about the one who broke them, until it was said to them: "We heard Abraham condemning them, so perhaps he is the one who broke them." So in one passage they witnessed him breaking them, and in the other they inferred from his condemnation of them that he was the one who broke them.

I say: there are two possible answers. The first is that those who saw him and rushed towards him were a small group of them, not the majority or their leaders. When the majority and the nobles returned from their festival to the house of the idols, to eat the food they had placed there seeking blessing from it, and they saw the idols broken, they were disgusted and asked, "Who has done this to them?" Then that small group did not inform on him openly, but by way of allusion and indirect hint, saying "We heard a youth mention them," because of some obstacles. The second is that he broke them and left without anyone noticing, and their rushing towards him came after they returned from their festival and asked about the one who broke them. Their words, "They said: Bring him before the eyes of the people," are also relevant here.

﴿وَاللَّهُ خَلَقَكُمْ وَمَا تَعْمَلُونَ﴾: meaning, He created you and what you make, that is, the idols you fashion. This is like His saying, ﴿Nay, your Lord is the Lord of the heavens and the earth, who created them﴾, meaning He created the idols.

If you ask: how can one and the same thing be created by God and be made by them, since He attributed both the creating and their making to it together?

I answer: this is like saying, "The carpenter made the door," and "the goldsmith made the bracelet and the anklet." What is meant is the making of the forms and shapes of these things, not their substances. The idols are substances and forms. The Creator of their substances is God, and those who make their forms are the ones who shape them by carving and by removing some of their parts, until the shape they want is achieved.

[Commentator's note: Zamakhshari quotes himself: "He means, He created you and what you make of idols, like His saying, 'Nay, your Lord is the Lord of the heavens and the earth, who created them.' If you ask how one thing can be created by God Most High and made by them, he answered that this is like saying, 'The carpenter made the door' ... up to his saying: '...and this unravels the composition and breaks it apart, as it would if you made it a verbal noun (maṣdariyyah).'" Ahmad (Ibn al-Munayyir) said: "If the torrent of God comes, the torrent of Ma'qil departs. We say that it is necessary to read it as a verbal noun (maṣdariyyah), because they did not worship these idols insofar as they were stones that were not shaped. Had that been so, they would not have cooperated in shaping them, nor would they have singled out one stone for worship over another. This shows that they worshipped them only in view of their shapes and forms, which are the traces of their work. In reality, then, they worshipped their own work, and the proof is established against them that they are like it. Moreover, the object of worship is the worshipper's acquisition and work. It is thus evident that the proof stands against them, and is clearer and more forceful, if ma is taken as a verbal noun. Once this is established, his argument should be refuted point by point. As for his saying that it is a relative pronoun, and that by their work on it is meant the work on its shapes, this contradicts the apparent sense, for it requires the deletion of a modifying noun in a place where that is not appropriate, so that the meaning would be: 'God created you and what you make of its shape and form.' By contrast, the interpretation of the People of the Sunnah requires no deletion at all. Furthermore, if the object of worship is taken to be the substance itself, how does this match their rebuke by showing that the object of worship is the worshipper's work, given that he concedes that the substances of the idols are not their work? What is their work, namely the shape, is not what they worship on this interpretation, and what they worship, namely the substance of the idol, is not their work. So on his interpretation the claim that the object of worship is the worshipper's work finds no firm footing. On what we have established, this becomes clear. As for his saying that the correspondence between 'what you carve' and 'what you make' breaks down under the interpretation of the People of the Sunnah, this is incorrect. We may read the first as a verbal noun, and that in reality they worshipped their carving, because these idols, which were stones before being carved, were not worshipped by them. When they worked on them with carving, they worshipped them. So in reality they worshipped nothing but their carving, which is their work. The correspondence is therefore present, and the argument is stronger and more binding in this case. Had it been as he said, the proof would have stood for them, and they would have said, as al-Zamakhshari says, contesting His saying, 'God created you and what you make,' by saying, 'No, and there is no honor in that. God does not create what we make; we only made the shaping and forming, and God did not create this.' They would have found a pretext to break into the argument. But God refuses except that the conclusive proof be ours and that the empty falsehoods be theirs. This is a binding argument, indeed a bridle for whoever opposes the Sunnah, a yoke on his neck, a wound to his shoulder, and a blow to his hand, until he returns to the truth repentant and admits his error in repentance."]

Al-Kursi (the chair) and the goldsmith's bracelet and anklet are examples of the same usage.

If you ask: why did you not reject the possibility that ma is a verbal noun rather than a relative pronoun, so that the meaning would be: "God created you and your work," as the Mujbirah say? [Editor's note: he means Ahl al-Sunnah, who held that there is no creator but God, so He is the creator of the servant's act. The Mu'tazilah (the Mu'tazilites) said that the servant is the creator of his own act, thereby making the servant a partner of God in creating, though they called themselves the people of justice and monotheism. They said: if God were the creator of the servant's act, then punishing the servant for sins would be injustice, not justice. The People of the Sunnah answered: He punishes him for them just as He rewards him for obedience, because the servant has acquisition (kasb) and choice in both, so there is no injustice. But the Mu'tazilah did not consider monotheism with full consideration, nor did they examine its proofs with full insight. (E.)]

I answer: the closest way to refute this objection, after it is refuted by the proofs of reason and the Book, is that the meaning of the verse rejects it plainly and clearly repudiates it. God, Mighty and Majestic, has argued against them that both the worshipper and the worshipped are God's creation. How, then, could a created thing worship a created thing? Moreover, the worshipper among them is the one who made the image and shape of the worshipped, and without him he could not have shaped and formed it himself. Suppose you said: "God created you and the creation of your work," and He had not argued against them; your speech would then not correspond. [Editor's note: it suffices for the argument that God is the creator of them and of their works in the idols and other things, and the idols create nothing. Sole creatorship is a stronger proof of sole divinity. (E.)]

Another point: His saying ﴿وَمَا تَعْمَلُونَ﴾ corresponds to His saying ﴿مَا تَنْحِتُونَ﴾, and the ma in ﴿مَا تَنْحِتُونَ﴾ is undoubtedly a relative pronoun. So none but a biased partisan of his own school, who ignores the science of rhetoric and does not perceive the composition of the Qur'an, would depart from its counterpart.

If you say: make it a relative pronoun so that the consequence I drew does not apply to me, and mean: "what you make of your works." I answer: rather, both consequences are around your neck, and only submission to the truth can free you from them. For even if you make it a relative pronoun, when you intend by it the work, you are not making an argument against the polytheists, just as you were not when you made it a verbal noun. Furthermore, you thereby sever the connection between "what you make" and "what you carve," by contrasting the two meanings: you mean by "what you carve" the concrete objects, which are the idols, and by "what you make" the abstract meanings, which are the works. This unravels the composition and breaks it apart, just as it would if you made it a verbal noun.

Al-Jahim: the blazing fire, intensely fueled. It is also said: any fire upon fire, and embers upon embers, is a jahim.

The meaning is that God, exalted is He, overcame them in both positions, and humbled them before Him. They wanted to overcome him by argument, so God gave him the words and inspired him with what silenced them, stoning them with proof. They were defeated and turned to scheming, so God nullified their scheme and made them the lowest and most debased, unable to prevail over him.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 37, verses 99–101:

He intended by his going to his Lord: his migration to where He commanded him to migrate to Him, from the land of Sham (Syria), as He said: ﴿Indeed, I am migrating to my Lord.﴾ ﴿He will guide me﴾: He will guide me to what is good for me in my religion, will protect me, and will grant me success, just as Moses, peace be upon him, said: ﴿No! Indeed, with me is my Lord; He will guide me.﴾ It is as if God had promised him and said to him: "I will guide you," so he related his words according to the manner of his Lord's promise. Or it is based on God's custom with him in guiding and directing him.

Or by this he displayed his trust (tawakkul) and his entrusting of his affair to God. Had he intended hope and expectation, he would have said, as Moses, peace be upon him, said: ﴿It may be that my Lord will guide me to the right path.﴾ ﴿Grant me [a child] from among the righteous.﴾ Grant me some of the righteous, meaning a child, because the word hibah (granting) has become predominant for a child, although it has also come for a brother in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We granted him, out of Our mercy, his brother Aaron as a prophet.﴾ He, mighty and majestic, said: ﴿And We granted him Isaac and Jacob﴾ and ﴿And We granted him John.﴾ 'Ali ibn Abi Talib said to Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, when he congratulated him on his child, "Abu al-Amlak": "You have thanked the Giver, and blessing has been placed upon you in what was given." For this reason the names Hibat Allah (Gift of God), Mawhub, Wahib and Mawhib came to be used. The glad tidings contained three things: that the child is a male boy, that he will reach the age of discernment (ḥilm), and that he will be forbearing (ḥalīm). And what forbearance is greater than his forbearance when his father proposed to slaughter him, and he said: ﴿You will find me, God willing, among the steadfast,﴾ and then submitted to that. It was said: God did not describe the prophets, peace be upon them, with anything less than He described them with forbearance, and that is because its existence is rare. God described Abraham with it in His saying: ﴿Indeed, Abraham was compassionate and forbearing﴾ and ﴿Indeed, Abraham was forbearing, compassionate, and turning back (to God).﴾ Because the event bore witness to the forbearance of both of them together.

When he reached the age of exertion along with him (ma‘ahu, "along with him"), that is, to help his father in his affairs and needs. If you ask: with what is ma‘ahu connected? I answer: it must be connected either to balagha (reached), or to al-sa‘y (exertion), or to some omitted element. It cannot be connected to balagha, because that would require that both of them reach the limit of exertion together; nor to al-sa‘y, because the complement of a verbal noun (masdar) may not precede it. Therefore it remains that it is an explanatory element (bayan), as if He had said: "When he reached al-sa‘y", meaning the limit at which he was able to exert himself; it is then asked: "With whom?" and He says: "With his father." The meaning of singling out the father is that he was the most gentle of people toward him and the most tender toward him, whereas others might have been harsh with him in demanding effort, and he would not have borne it, because his strength had not yet become firm and his stature had not yet hardened. At that time he was thirteen years old. The intent is that, despite the tenderness of his age and his being in the stage of childhood, he possessed a steadiness of forbearance and a breadth of breast which emboldened him to bear that great trial and to give that wise reply: he was shown in a dream, and it was said to him: "Slaughter your son." The dreams of prophets are revelation, like revelation in wakefulness. Therefore he said: "Indeed I see in a dream that I am slaughtering you," and so he mentioned the interpretation of the dream, just as the one being tested, who has seen that he is riding in a ship, says: "I saw in a dream that I am saved from this ordeal."

It is also said: he saw on the night of tarwiyah (the eighth of Dhu al-Hijjah) as if someone were saying to him: "Indeed God commands you to slaughter this son of yours." When he awoke he pondered this all morning until evening, asking whether this dream was from God or from Satan. Hence the day was named Tarwiyah (the day of pondering). When he evening came, he saw the like of it, and he knew that it was from God; hence the day was named ʿArafah (the day of knowing). Then he saw the like of it on the third night, and he resolved to slaughter him, so the day was named the Day of Sacrifice (Yawm al-Nahr).

It is also said: when the angels gave him the good news of a forbearing boy, he said: "Then he is the sacrificed one of God (dhabih Allah)." When he was born and reached the age of exertion with him, it was said to him: "Fulfil your vow," so: "Consider what you see," that is, by way of consultation, what opinion you hold and display. It is also read: "mā tarā" (what you see), i.e., what you perceive of your own opinion and reveal. And "mā tarā," read in the passive, means: what you show yourself of opinion. "Do what you are commanded" means: what you are commanded to do, so the preposition is omitted, as it is omitted in the verse of the poet:

"I commanded you good, so do what you were commanded (bihi)"

Or "amruka" is in the sense of the verbal noun with its object, and the thing commanded is called a command. It is also read: "mā tu'mar bihi."

If you ask: why did he consult him about a matter which was a binding decree from God? I answer: he did not consult him in order to return to his opinion and counsel, but in order to know what was in him regarding the trial from God that had befallen him, so that He might steady his footing and make him patient if he became distressed, and be secure from his slipping if he endured and submitted. He also wished to inform him so that he would reflect upon himself, prepare his soul, make it easy for her, and meet the trial as one already at ease with it; and so that he would earn reward by submitting to God's command before it descended. Furthermore, slaughtering someone by surprise (al-mughafasah) is something deemed ugly; and so that it would become a tradition in consultation. For it has been said: had Adam consulted the angels about eating from the tree, he would not have erred in that.

If you ask: why was that through a dream rather than in wakefulness? I answer: just as God showed Joseph, peace be upon him, the prostration of his parents and brothers to him in a dream without a revelation to his father; and just as the Messenger of God (ﷺ) promised entry into the Sacred Mosque in a dream; and other dreams of the prophets besides these. This is to strengthen the evidence that they are truthful and believed, because the state is either a state of wakefulness or a state of sleep, and when both states agree in truthfulness, that is stronger evidence than either one alone.

It is said: "Salima li-amr Allah" (he submitted to the command of God), "aslama" and "istaslama" have one meaning, and all three have been recited, when he yields to Him and humbles himself. Its origin is your saying: "salima hadha li-fulan" (this became pure for so-and-so) when it was free for him. Its meaning is: it was safe from being disputed. The sayings "salima li-amr Allah" and "aslama lahu" are derived from it, and the real meaning of both is: he sincerely devoted himself to God and made himself safe and sincere for Him. Likewise the meaning of "istaslama" is: he singled out his self for God.

From Qatadah, regarding ﴿أَسْلَمَا﴾ (both had submitted): this one (Abraham) submitted his son, and this one (Ishmael) submitted himself. ﴿وَتَلَّهُ لِلْجَبِينِ﴾ (and he threw him down on his forehead): he cast him down on his side, so one of his two temples fell upon the ground, in humility [[قوله «تواضعا على مباشرة الأمر» أى توافقا. (ع)]] before undertaking the matter, with patience and fortitude, seeking to please the Most Merciful and to disgrace Satan. It is narrated that this took place at the rock that is in Mina. From al-Hasan: at the place overlooking the Mosque of Mina. From al-Dahhak: at the place of sacrifice where people sacrifice today.

If you say: where is the answer (jawab) of "lamma"? I say: it is omitted, and its estimate is: "fa-lamma aslama wa-tallahu lil-jabin wa-nadaynahu an ya Ibrahim, qad saddaqta al-ru'ya" (so when they had submitted and he had thrown him down on his forehead, and We called out to him: "O Abraham, you have fulfilled the vision"), there occurred what occurred, which the state speaks of and which description cannot encompass, of their joy and gladness, their praise of God and their thanks for what He bestowed upon them, by averting the great trial after it had descended, and by what they gained amid it by settling their souls upon it, of reward and recompense and the good pleasure of God, beyond which there is no sought-after thing. And His saying ﴿إِنَّا كَذَلِكَ نَجْزِي الْمُحْسِنِينَ﴾ (Indeed, thus do We reward the good-doers) is a cause (ta'lil) for the bestowal of what He granted them of relief after hardship, and of attaining the desired aim after despair. ﴿الْبَلَاءُ الْمُبِينُ﴾ (the manifest trial): the clear test by which the sincere are distinguished from others, or the manifest ordeal whose difficulty has no greater ordeal than it.

"Al-dhibh" (the sacrifice): the name of what is slaughtered. From Ibn Abbas, may God be pleased with them both: it was the ram which Abel offered, and it was accepted from him, and it used to graze in Paradise until Ishmael was ransomed with it. From al-Hasan: he was ransomed with a [[قوله «بو عل» في الصحاح: الوعل: الأروى اه، ويقال: التيس الجبلي. (ع)]] wild goat that descended upon him from Thabir. From Ibn Abbas: had that sacrifice been completed, it would have become a sunnah, and people would have slaughtered their sons.

﴿عَظِيمٍ﴾ (great): large in body and fat. This is the sunnah in sacrifices (udhiyah). And his peace be upon him said: "Pick out your sacrificial animals, for they are your mounts over the Bridge (sirat)." It was also said: because it occurred as a ransom for the son of Abraham. It is narrated that it fled from Abraham, peace be upon him, at the Jamrah, so he struck it with seven pebbles until he caught it, and therefore it became a sunnah in throwing (the pebbles). It is also narrated that he threw at Satan when Satan appeared to him with whisperings at the slaughter of his son. It is narrated that when he slaughtered him, Gabriel said: "Allahu akbar, Allahu akbar," and the one to be sacrificed said: "La ilaha illa Allah, wallahu akbar," and Abraham, peace be upon him, said: "Allahu akbar, wa-lillahi al-hamd" [[لم أجده.]], so it became a sunnah.

It is related in the story of the sacrificed one (al-dhabih) that when he (Abraham) wanted to slaughter him, he said: "O my son, take the rope and the knife and let us set out to the ravine to gather firewood." When he reached the middle of the ravine of Thabir, he informed him of what he had been commanded. He (the son) said: "Tighten my bonds so that I do not thrash about; hold your garments away from me so that nothing of my blood spatters upon them, lest my reward be diminished and my mother see it and grieve; sharpen your blade and hasten its passage over my throat so that it finishes me quickly, for it will be easier, since death is severe; and convey my greetings to my mother, and if you see fit to return my shirt to my mother, do so, for perhaps it will be easier for her." Abraham, peace be upon him, said: "What a fine helper you are, O my son, in the command of God." Then he approached him, kissing him while he had bound him, and both of them were weeping. Then he placed the knife upon his throat, but it did not cut, because God had placed a sheet of copper upon his throat. He (the son) said to him: "Lay me on my face, for when you look at my face you will be moved to mercy, and tenderness will overtake you and come between you and the command of God." He did so. Then he placed the knife upon his nape, and the knife turned over, and it was called out: "O Abraham, you have fulfilled the vision." He looked, and there was Gabriel, peace be upon him, with a white-black horned ram, and Gabriel and the ram pronounced "Allahu akbar," and Abraham and his son (did so too), and he came to the place of sacrifice in Mina and slaughtered it. It was also said: when the place of prostration of him (the son) reached the ground, relief came.

Abu Hanifah, may God have mercy on him, cited this verse regarding one who vows to slaughter his son: that it obliges him to slaughter a sheep. If you say: which of his two sons was the sacrificed one? I say: this has been disputed. From Ibn Abbas, Ibn Umar, Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi and a group of the Successors (tabi'un): it was Ishmael. The proof for this is that the Messenger of God ﷺ said: "I am the son of the two sacrificed ones" (ana ibn al-dhabihayn). And a Bedouin said to him: "O son of the two sacrificed ones," and he smiled, and he was asked about that, and he said: "When Abd al-Muttalib dug the well of Zamzam, he vowed to God that if God facilitated its affair for him, he would surely sacrifice one of his sons. The lot fell upon Abdullah, but his maternal uncles prevented him and said to him: 'Ransom your son with a hundred camels,' and he ransomed him with a hundred camels. The second one is Ishmael." [[أخرجه الحاكم والثعلبي من رواية الصنابحى عن معاوية رضى الله عنه وفيه قصة.]]

And from Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi, he said: "The most devout of the Children of Israel used to say when he supplicated: 'O God, the God of Abraham, Ishmael and Israel.' Moses, peace be upon him, said: 'O Lord, what is the matter with the most devout of the Children of Israel, that when he supplicates he says: O God, the God of Abraham, Ishmael and Israel, while I am among them? Have You not made me hear Your speech and chosen me with Your message?' He said: 'O Moses, none has loved Me as Abraham loved Me, ever; and I have never been presented with a choice between Myself and anything else except that he chose Me. As for Ishmael, he gave the blood of his own self generously. As for Israel, he never despaired of My mercy in any hardship that ever befell him.' This is supported by the fact that when God, exalted is He, completed the story of the sacrificed one, He said: ﴿وَبَشَّرْنَاهُ بِإِسْحَاقَ نَبِيًّا﴾ (And We gave him the good news of Isaac, a prophet)." And from Muhammad ibn Ka'b, that he said to Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz: "It is Ishmael." Umar said: "This is a matter I had not considered, and indeed I see it as you have said." Then he sent for a Jew who had embraced Islam and asked him, and he said: "Indeed the Jews know that it is Ishmael, but they envy you, O Arabs." And this is supported by the fact that the two horns of the ram were hung in the Ka'bah in the hands of the sons of Ishmael until the House burned. And from al-Asma'i, he said: "I asked Abu Amr ibn al-Ala' about the sacrificed one, and he said: 'O Asma'i, where has your intellect strayed? When was Isaac in Mecca? Ishmael was in Mecca; he is the one who built the House with his father, and the place of sacrifice is in Mecca.'"

And among what indicates it is that God described him with patience, unlike his brother Isaac, in His saying ﴿وَإِسْمَاعِيلَ وَإِدْرِيسَ وَذَا الْكِفْلِ كُلٌّ مِنَ الصَّابِرِينَ﴾ (And Ishmael, and Idris, and Dhul-Kifl; each of them was among the patient), and that is his patience in the slaughter; and He described him with truthfulness of promise in His saying ﴿إِنَّهُ كَانَ صَادِقَ الْوَعْدِ﴾ (Indeed, he was true to his promise), because he promised his father to be patient of himself in the slaughter, and he fulfilled it. And because God gave him the good news of Isaac and of Isaac's son Jacob in His saying ﴿فَضَحِكَتْ فَبَشَّرْنَاهَا بِإِسْحَاقَ وَمِنْ وَرَاءِ إِسْحَاقَ يَعْقُوبَ﴾ (So she laughed, and We gave her the good news of Isaac, and after Isaac, Jacob). So if the sacrificed one were Isaac, it would have been a breach of the promise regarding Jacob. And from Ali ibn Abi Talib, Ibn Mas'ud, al-Abbas, Ata, Ikrimah and a group of the Successors: it was Isaac. The proof for this is that God, exalted is He, informed about His friend Abraham when he migrated to Syria, that he asked Him for a son, then followed that with the good news of a forbearing boy, then mentioned his vision of slaughtering that boy who had been given good news of. It is also supported by the letter of Jacob to Joseph: "From Jacob, Israel of God, son of Isaac, the sacrificed one of God, son of Abraham, friend of God" [[أخرجه الترمذي في النوادر في الحادي والعشرين بعد المائتين: حدثنا عمر بن أبى عمر حدثنا عصام بن المثنى الحمصي عن أبيه عن وهب بن منبه قال «كتب يعقوب كتابا فيه: بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم. من يعقوب نبى الله إلى آخره» وأخرج الدارقطني في غرائب مالك من رواية إسحاق بن وهب الطوسي عن ابن وهب عن مالك عن نافع عن ابن عمر رفعه «أوحى إلى ملك الموت أن ائت يعقوب فسلم عليه فذكر الحديث- وفيه فقال: اكتبوا بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم من يعقوب إسرائيل الله بن إسحاق ذبيح الله بن إبراهيم خليل الله إلى عزيز مصر أما بعد فانا أهل بيت فذكره مطولا. قال الدارقطني: هذا موضوع. وإسحاق كان يضع الحديث على ابن وهب. وقد تقدم في يوسف من وجه آخر.]].

If you say: God had revealed to Abraham, upon him be blessings of God, in a dream that he should slaughter his son, and he did not slaughter him, and it was said to him: "You have fulfilled the vision," and he would only have fulfilled it if the slaughter had been valid from him, but it was not valid. [[قال محمود: «فان قلت قد أوحى إلى إبراهيم في المنام أن يذبح ولده ولم يذبح، وقيل له: قد صدقت الرؤيا وإنما كان يصدقها لو صح منه الذبح، ولم يصح. فأجاب بأنه قد بذل وسعه وفعل ما يفعله الذابح من بطحه على شقه وإمرار الشفرة على حلقه، ولكن الله سبحانه منع الشفرة أن تمضى فيه وهذا لا يقدح في فعل إبراهيم، ألا ترى أنه لا يسمى عاصيا ولا مفرطا بل يسمى مطيعا ومجتهدا، كما لو مضت فيه الشفرة وفرت الأوداج وأنهرت الدم، وليس هذا من ورود النسخ على المأمور به قبل الفعل ولا قل أوان الفعل في شيء، كما يسبق إلى بعض الأوهام حتى يشتغل بالكلام عليه. انتهى كلامه» قال أحمد: كل ما ذكر دندنة حول امتناع النسخ قبل التمكن من الفعل، وتلك قاعدة المعتزلة. وأما أهل السنة فيثبتون جوازه، لأن التكليف ثابت قبل التمكن من الفعل، فجاز رفعه كالموت. وأيضا فكل نسخ كذلك، لأن القدرة على الفعل عندنا مقارنة لا متقدمة، ثم يثبتون وقوعه بهذه الآية. ووجه الدليل منها أن إبراهيم عليه السلام أمر بالذبح بدليل افْعَلْ ما تُؤْمَرُ ونسخ قبل التمكن بدليل العدول إلى الفداء، فمن ثم تحوم الزمخشري على أنه فعل غاية وسعه من بطحه على شقه وإمرار الشفرة على حلقه، وإنما امتنعت بأمر من الله تعالى، وغرضه بذلك أحد أمرين: إما أن يكون الأمر إنما توجه عليه بمقدمات الذبح وقد حصلت لا بنفس الذبح، أو توجه الأمر بنفس الذبح وتعاطيه، ولكن لم يتمكن. وكلا الأمرين لا يخلصه. أما قوله: أمر بمقدمات الذبح فباطل بقوله إِنِّي أَرى فِي الْمَنامِ أَنِّي أَذْبَحُكَ وقوله افْعَلْ ما تُؤْمَرُ وأما قوله: لم يتمكن لأن الشفرة منعت بأمر من الله تعالى بعد تسليم الأمر بالذبح، فحاصله أنه لم يتمكن من الذبح المأمور به، فكان النسخ إذا قبل التمكن، وهو عين ما أنكره المعتزلة، ولما لم يكن في هذين الجوابين لهم خلاص: لجأ بعضهم إلى تسليم أنه أمر بالذبح، ودعوى أنه ذبح ولكنه كان يلتحم، وهو باطل لا ثبوت له. وسياق الآية يخل دعواه ويفل ثنياه.]] I say: he exerted his utmost effort and did what the slaughterer does, by laying him on his side and passing the blade over his throat, but God, glorified is He, brought about what prevented the blade from passing through him. This does not detract from the act of Abraham, peace be upon him. Do you not see that he is not called disobedient nor negligent, but is called obedient and striving, just as if the blade had passed through him, the windpipes had been severed and the blood had flowed? This is not the case of abrogation (naskh) of a command before its performance, nor before the time of its performance in any respect, as some fancies might come to mind, so that one occupies oneself with discussing it. 

If you say: God is the one from whom the ransom is sought, since He is the one who commanded the slaughter, so how can He be the ransomer, to the extent that He said ﴿وَفَدَيْنَاهُ﴾ (And We ransomed him)? I say: the ransomer is Abraham, peace be upon him, and God, mighty and majestic is He, granted him the ram so that he might ransom with it. He said ﴿وَفَدَيْنَاهُ﴾ (We ransomed him) ascribing the ransom to the cause, which is the enabling of the ransom through His granting it. 

If you say: then if what Abraham did of laying him down and passing the blade is in the status of slaughter, what is the meaning of ransom, when ransom is only the release from slaughter by a substitute? I say: it is known, by God's prevention, that the reality of slaughter was not achieved through severing the windpipes and the flow of blood. So God granted him the ram so that its slaughter would stand in place of that reality, so that that reality would not occur in the person of Ishmael, but in the person of the ram as a substitute for him.

If you say: what is the benefit in that reality being realized, since it has already been dispensed with by what Abraham did standing in place of slaughter without any deficiency? I say: the benefit in that is that what was prevented would be realized in its substitute, so that the fulfilment of the vow and the performance of the command would be complete in every respect.

If you say: why was it said here ﴿كَذَلِكَ نَجْزِي الْمُحْسِنِينَ﴾ (thus do We reward the good-doers), and in other stories: ﴿إِنَّا كَذَلِكَ﴾ (indeed, thus)? I say: ﴿إِنَّا كَذَلِكَ﴾ has already preceded in this story, so it was as if the omission of it (the second "inna") was lightened by mentioning it once rather than mentioning it a second time.

It is said: "Salima li-amr Allah" (he submitted to the command of God), "aslama" and "istaslama" have one meaning, and all three have been recited, when he yields to Him and humbles himself. Its origin is your saying: "salima hadha li-fulan" (this became pure for so-and-so) when it was free for him. Its meaning is: it was safe from being disputed. The sayings "salima li-amr Allah" and "aslama lahu" are derived from it, and the real meaning of both is: he sincerely devoted himself to God and made himself safe and sincere for Him.
