﴿So ask them﴾ is coordinated with a similar phrase at the beginning of the surah, even though a long distance separates them. He commanded His Messenger to ask the Quraysh first about the manner in which they denied the resurrection. Then the discourse continued, one part joined to another, and He commanded him to ask them about the unjust division (al-qisma al-dayzā) that they made, when they assigned daughters to God and sons to themselves, in their saying that the angels are the daughters of God. This was despite their intense aversion to daughters, their burying of them alive, and their disdain for mentioning them.

In this they committed three kinds of disbelief. The first is tajsīm (anthropomorphism, ascribing bodily form to God), because childbearing belongs only to bodies. The second is preferring themselves over their Lord, when they assigned to Him the lower of the two sexes and to themselves the higher, as He said: ﴿When one of them is given the good news of that which he attributes to the Most Merciful, his face becomes darkened, and he suppresses his grief. Is one who is brought up among ornaments, and who in dispute is not clear?﴾ The third is that they belittled the most noble of God's creation and those nearest to Him, by making them female. If it were said to the least and lowest of them, "There is femininity in you," or "Your form is the form of women," the speaker would be made to wear the skin of a leopard, and the pupils of his eyes would turn over [[The note: "ولانقلبت حماليقه" in al-Ṣiḥāḥ (the lexicon of al-Jawharī) reads "ḥimlāq al-ʿayn": the inner part of the eyelids, which is blackened by kohl. End of note (ʿ).]]. Such things appear openly in their satires. Therefore God repeated all these kinds in His Book many times, and He showed their gravity in verses: ﴿And they say, "The Most Merciful has taken a son." Indeed you have produced something monstrous.﴾ ﴿The heavens almost burst apart from it.﴾ ﴿And they say, "The Most Merciful has taken a son." Glory be to Him! Rather, they are honored servants.﴾ ﴿And they say, "God has taken a son." Glory be to Him! Rather, to Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth. Originator of the heavens and the earth, how could He have a son?﴾ ﴿Unquestionably, it is from their own falsehood that they say, "God has begotten a son," and indeed they are liars.﴾ ﴿And they have made for Him a portion from His servants.﴾ ﴿And they attribute to God daughters, glory be to Him, while for themselves is what they desire.﴾ ﴿Has He chosen daughters over sons? What is the matter with you? **Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on Surah 37, verses 158–160:**

They made between God and the jinn a kinship (*nasab*). And "the angels" is what they claimed: that they are His daughters. The meaning is: by what they said, they established a kinship between God and themselves, and by this they affirmed for Him a common kind that includes Him and the angels.

If you ask: why did He call the angels "jinn"? I answer: they said the kind is one, but whoever among the jinn was corrupt and rebellious, and was entirely evil, is a devil (*shaytan*), and whoever among them was pure, devout, and entirely good, is an angel (*malak*). So He mentioned them in this place by the name of their kind, and He mentioned them by this name to lower them and to belittle them, even though they (the angels) were magnified in their own selves, so that they would not reach the rank of kinship which they (the disbelievers) attributed to them. In this there is an indication that whoever has the attribute of concealment and hiddenness, which is a property of bodies, is not fit to be related to one who cannot be described by that. An example of this: you equate the king with one of his special and close associates, and he says to you: "Do you equate me with my servant?" And when he mentions him in other than this position, he honors him and gives him a kunya.

The pronoun in *innahum la-muhdarun* ("indeed they will be brought forth") refers to the disbelievers. The meaning is: they say what they say about the angels, while the angels know that in this they are liars and fabricators, and that they will be brought forth to the Fire and punished for what they say. The intent is to emphasize the denial, since it is attributed to the knowledge of those whom they claimed that kinship for.

It has been said: they said that God intermarried with the jinn, and from that the angels came forth. It has also been said: they said that God and Satan are brothers.

It is reported from al-Hasan: they associated the jinn with obedience to God.

It is permissible, if *al-jinna* is interpreted as the devils, for the pronoun in *innahum la-muhdarun* to refer to them (the devils), and the meaning would be that the devils know that God will bring them forth to the Fire and punish them; and if they were related to Him, or partners in the obligation of obedience, He would not have punished them.

*Illa 'ibad Allah al-mukhlasin* ("except the sincere servants of God") is an exceptive clause that is disjunctive from "the ones brought forth." Its meaning: "but the sincere ones are saved." *Subhan Allah* ("Glory be to God") is a parenthetical interjection between the exception and what preceded it.

It is permissible that the exception be from the *waw* in *yasifun* ("they describe"), meaning: these people describe Him with that, but the sincere ones are free from describing Him with it.

The pronoun in ʿalayhi refers to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and its meaning is: ﴿Indeed you and what you worship are not, all of you, going to tempt [anyone] against Allah, except those destined for the Fire, whose [end] was foreknown in His knowledge, that because of the evil of their deeds they deserve to burn in it.﴾

If you ask: how can they tempt them against Allah? I answer: they corrupt them against Him by their misguiding and mockery. This is like your saying, "So-and-so tempted so-and-so's wife against him," just as you say, "He spoiled her for him and made her unfit for him."

It is also permissible for the waw in ﴿wa mā taʿbudūn﴾ to mean "with," as in their saying, "Every man and his property" (kull rajul wa ḍayʿatuhu). Just as it is permissible to stop at "every man" and to say "and his property" separately, so it is permissible to stop at His saying ﴿fa-innakum﴾, because His saying ﴿wa mā taʿbudūn﴾ takes the place of the predicate, since its meaning is: "Indeed you, together with what you worship." The meaning is: "Indeed you, together with your gods, that is, you are their companions and associates, not ceasing to worship them." Then He said ﴿mā antum ʿalayhi﴾, that is, concerning what you worship, ﴿bi-fātinīn﴾, meaning, inciting or inducing [others] to the path of temptation and misguidance, ﴿illā man huwa ṣāl mithlakum﴾, meaning, except those who, like you, are themselves astray.

Or it may be in the style of the verse:

*"Indeed you, along with the book reaching ʿAlī, are like a woman tanning a hide, while the hide has already rotted and the tanning did not benefit it."*

This verse is attributed to ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ, and it was also said to be [composed] for al-Walīd ibn ʿUqba ibn Abī Muʿayṭ, urging Muʿāwiya to fight ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib. (The verb ḥalama, said of a hide, means that it has rotted and become rotten and perforated.) Ḥalama with a ḍamma (ḥulm) and with a kasra in the infinitive means "to forgive while having the power [to punish]." Ḥalama with a fatḥa in the perfect and a ḍamma in the infinitive means "to see something in one's dream." The poet says: "Indeed you and your book reaching ʿAlī, which you hope will set it right, are like a man who tans hides much, or like a woman who tans it, while the hide has already gone bad and the tanning has not helped it." The purpose is to compare one state with another. It is also permissible that the waw is for accompaniment ("with") and not for conjunction, so the meaning is comparing Muʿāwiya to the tanning woman.

Al-Ḥasan recited ﴿ṣāl al-jaḥīm﴾ with a ḍamma on the lām. In this reading there are three possibilities. The first is that it is a plural, with the waw dropped because two unvocalized letters met (the waw and the definite article lām). If you ask how the plural fits with His saying ﴿man huwa﴾, I answer: the word "man" is singular in form but plural in meaning, so ﴿huwa﴾ is taken according to its form, and "the ones who are astray" (al-ṣāliḥūn, the plural form) is taken according to its meaning, just as in some places of the revelation the form of "man" is taken in one verse and its meaning in the same verse. The second possibility is that the original is ṣāʾil, changed by metathesis, and then ṣāl is said, as in their saying shākk fī shāʾik (the pattern of ṣāʾil to ṣāl). The third is that the lām of ṣāl is deleted for lightness, and the i'rab (grammatical inflection) is applied to its middle letter, as in their saying: "mā bālaytu bihi bālah," the original being bālīya from bālā, like ʿāfiyah from ʿāfā. A parallel to this is the recitation of the one who recited:

*"And the fruit of the two gardens is near, and the ships raised high (al-jawārī al-munshaʾāt)."*

in which the i'rab is applied to the middle letter.

Or it may be in the style of the verse:

*"Indeed you, along with the book reaching ʿAlī, are like a woman tanning a hide, while the hide has already rotted and the tanning did not benefit it."*

This verse is attributed to ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ, and it was also said to be [composed] for al-Walīd ibn ʿUqba ibn Abī Muʿayṭ, urging Muʿāwiya to fight ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib. (The verb ḥalama, said of a hide, means that it has rotted and become rotten and perforated.) Ḥalama with a ḍamma (ḥulm) and with a kasra in the infinitive means "to forgive while having the power [to punish]." Ḥalama with a fatḥa in the perfect and a ḍamma in the infinitive means "to see something in one's dream." The poet says: "Indeed you and your book reaching ʿAlī, which you hope will set it right, are like a man who tans hides much, or like a woman who tans it, while the hide has already gone bad and the tanning has not helped it." The purpose is to compare one state with another. It is also permissible that the waw is for accompaniment ("with") and not for conjunction, so the meaning is comparing Muʿāwiya to the tanning woman.

Al-Ḥasan recited ﴿ṣāl al-jaḥīm﴾ with a ḍamma on the lām. In this reading there are three possibilities. The second possibility is that the original is ṣāʾil, changed by metathesis, and then ṣāl is said, as in their saying shākk fī shāʾik (the pattern of ṣāʾil to ṣāl). *"And the fruit of the two gardens is near, and the ships raised high (al-jawārī al-munshaʾāt)."*

in which the i'rab is applied to the middle letter.

This is a commentary from al-Zamakhshari's *al-Kashshaf* on Surah 37, verses 164–166:

﴿There is none of us but has a known station﴾. Here the described noun is omitted and the attribute is placed in its position, as in the line of poetry:

"I am the son of Jala and the climber of the passes" [[The explanation of this line was given in volume 2, page 305. Refer to it if you wish. End of the corrector's note.]]

"With my hand, I was the best archer among people" [[The explanation of this line was given in volume 2, page 616. Refer to it if you wish. End of the corrector's note.]]

The "station" is a known station in worship, and the arrival at God's command is restricted to it and does not go beyond it, as is related: "Among them is one who bows and does not straighten his spine, and one who prostrates and does not raise his head." ﴿Indeed, we are those who line up﴾, placing our feet in prayer, or our wings in the air, awaiting what we are commanded. It was also said: we place half of our wings around the Throne, calling for blessings upon the believers. It was also said: the Muslims began to line up in prayer only since this verse was revealed, and no one among the people of other religions lines up in their prayers except the Muslims. ﴿And indeed, we are those who glorify﴾, meaning those who declare God free of imperfection, or those who pray.

The correct view is that this, and what precedes it in ﴿Glory be to God above what they describe﴾, is the speech of the angels, so that it connects with their mention in ﴿And the jinn certainly know﴾. It is as if it were said: the angels knew and witnessed that the polytheists were slandering them in relation to the Lord of Might, and they said "Glory be to God," declaring Him free of that, and they excluded the sincere servants of God and disassociated themselves from them. They said to the disbelievers: when this is established, you and your gods cannot cause any of God's creatures to stray or go astray, except one who is like you, whom God knows will disbelieve, not by His decree or will. [[The statement "not by His decree and will, exalted is He" is based on the position of the Mu'tazilites (al-Mu'tazilah, a theological school) that God does not decree or will evil. The People of the Sunnah (Ahl al-Sunnah) said: every existing thing occurs by God's decree and measure, as explained in the science of monotheism. (ʿ)]] Exalted is God above what the wrongdoers say, a great exaltation, that they are among the people of the Fire. How could we be related to the Lord of Might, when we and He are not of one kind? We are only humble servants before Him, each of us has a station of obedience from which he cannot deviate even a fingernail, out of humility before His greatness and submission to His majesty. We are those who line up our feet for His worship and our wings, submitting, humbled, glorifying and extolling Him, as servants must do before their Lord. [[The phrase "as servants must do before their Lord" may be "as must be done," like the wording of al-Nasafi. (ʿ)]]

It was also said: this is from the words of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), meaning: no one among the Muslims is without a known station on the Day of Resurrection according to his deeds, from His saying, ﴿It may be that your Lord will raise you to a praised station﴾. Then he mentioned their deeds, and that they are the ones who line up in prayer, glorifying God and declaring Him free of what the ignorant attribute to Him that is not permissible for Him.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 37, verses 167–170:

They are the polytheists of Quraysh. They used to say: ﴿If only we had with us a reminder (dhikr)﴾, meaning a book (kitab) from among the books of the former peoples, the ones to whom the Torah and the Gospel were sent, "we would have made our worship sincerely for God, and we would not have denied as they denied, nor opposed as they opposed." Then the Reminder came to them, the one that is the lord of reminders (sayyid al-adhkar), and the Book that is unparalleled (mu'jiz) among books, and they disbelieved in it. A similar verse is: ﴿But when a warner came to them, it increased them only in aversion﴾. ﴿So they will soon know the outcome (maghabba) of their denial and what punishment (intiqam) will befall them.﴾

In ﴿wa-in﴾, the particle is the lightened form (mukhaffafa) of the heavy (thaqila), and the lam is the distinguishing lam (al-lam al-fariqa). In this there is the point that they used to say this emphatically (mu'akkidin lil-qawl), earnestly (jaddin fihi), so how great is the difference between the beginning of their affair and its end.

The Word: His saying, "Indeed they will be the ones given victory, and indeed Our host will be the ones who prevail." He called it "a word" (kalimah) though it consists of several words, because when they were gathered into one meaning they took the status of a single word. It has been read as "kalimatuna" (Our words). The intended meaning is the promise of their superiority over their enemies in the battles of argument and the fierce encounters of war in this world, and their superiority over them in the Hereafter, as He said: ﴿And those who have taquwa will be above them on the Day of Resurrection﴾. This does not necessarily conflict with their being defeated in some encounters, or with some of them being killed, for the victory belonged to them and to those who came after them in the final outcome. The examples of the battles of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the Rightly Guided Caliphs suffice as a model to follow and a lesson to learn from. It is related from al-Hasan (may Allah have mercy on him): "No prophet was ever defeated in war, nor was any killed in it." Moreover, the foundation and basis of their affair, and what predominates in it, is triumph and victory, even if some trial and affliction occur in the course of it, and the ruling belongs to the one who prevails. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both): "If they are not helped in this world, they will be helped in the Hereafter." In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: "for Our servants," with the verb "sabaqat" construed to include the sense of "haqqat" (it has become binding).

Then turn away from them and overlook them, [[His saying "and overlook their harm" — in al-Sihah: "al-ighda'" means lowering the eyelids. (ʿ)]] for a while, meaning for a short period, which is the period of refraining from fighting. From al-Suddi: until the day of Badr. It was also said: until death. And it was said: until the Day of Resurrection. And watch them, and what will be decreed against them of captivity, killing and punishment in the Hereafter; for they will soon see, and [watch] what will be decreed for you of victory, support and reward in the end. The purpose of the command to watch them, regarding the awaited and promised state, is to indicate that it will certainly come to pass, and that its occurrence is near, as if it were before your eyes.

In this there is consolation for him and relief for his distress. His saying "so they will soon see" is a threat, as has passed, and not for distance in time.

The punishment that descended upon them after they had been warned and had denied it is depicted as an army that gave its warning of attack to its people through some of its well-wishers. They paid no heed to the warning, did not prepare themselves, and did not devise any plan that might save them, until it halted in their courtyard suddenly, launched its raid upon them, and cut off their last trace. It was the custom of their raiders (maghawir) to attack at dawn, so the raid was named "dawn" (sabah) even when it occurred at another time. This verse does not attain its eloquence, nor does it have the awe that you feel and that its meaning delights you with in yourself and your nature, except because it comes in the manner of a parable (tamthil).

Ibn Mas'ud recited: "fa-bi'sa sabah" (so evil was the morning). It was also read as "nazala bi-saahatihim" (it descended into their courtyard), with the verb attributed to the prepositional phrase, as in your saying "dhahaba bi-Zayd" (Zayd went away) and "nazala" (he descended), on the basis of the line: "wa-nazala al-'adhab" (and the punishment descended).

The meaning is: "So evil is the morning of those who were warned, their morning." The lam in "al-mundhirin" (those who were warned) is indefinite in reference to the category of those who were warned, because the verbs sa'a (ساء) and bi'sa (بئس) require that.

It is said that it refers to the descent of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) in Mecca on the day of the conquest.

From Anas (may God be pleased with him): When the Messenger of God (ﷺ) came to Khaybar, and they had gone out to their fields carrying their hoes (al-masaahi), they said: "Muhammad and the army!" and they returned to their fortress. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Allahu akbar! Khaybar is ruined. Indeed, when we descend into the courtyard of a people, evil is the morning of those who were warned." [Agreed upon]

The repetition of "wa-tawalla 'anhum" (and turn away from them) serves as consolation upon consolation and as an emphasis on the certainty of the promise, adding emphasis upon emphasis. There is an additional benefit in it: the two verbs are used together without being restricted to an object, and it means that "they will see them and they will see" what cannot be encompassed by mention, of the various kinds of joy and the varieties of harm.

It is said that one of the two refers to the punishment of this world, and the other to the punishment of the Hereafter.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 37, verses 180–182:

The Lord (al-Rabb) is attributed to "might" (al-'izza) because He alone is characterized by it, as if it were said: "Possessor of might," just as you say "companion of truth" (sahib sidq), due to its being exclusive to him. It is also permissible that what is meant is that there is no might for any of the kings or others except that He is its Lord and its owner, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿You give might to whom You will﴾.

The surah included mention of what the polytheists said about God, and what they attributed to Him of things far removed from Him, and what the messengers suffered at their hands, and what was promised them in the end of victory over them. So it concluded with the comprehensive summary of that: the glorification of His essence above what the polytheists described Him with, and the greeting of peace upon the messengers, ﴿And praise belongs to God, Lord of the worlds﴾, for what He ordained for them of good outcomes. The purpose is to teach the believers to say this, not to neglect it, and not to be heedless of the contents of His noble Book and the deposits of His glorious Qur'an.

It is related from 'Ali, may God be pleased with him, that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Whoever loves to be given full measure of reward on the Day of Resurrection, let the last of his words when he rises from his assembly be:

﴿Glory be to your Lord, the Lord of might, above what they describe. And peace be upon the messengers. And praise belongs to God, Lord of the worlds.﴾" [[Narrated by 'Abd al-Razzaq and al-Tha'labi, from the narration of al-Asbagh ibn Nubata from 'Ali, as a mawquf (halting at 'Ali). Ibn Abi Hatim narrated it from the narration of al-Sha'bi from the Prophet (ﷺ) as a mursal (a hadith with a missing companion link).]] From the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "Whoever recites Surat al-Saffat will be given the reward of ten good deeds for each jinn and devil, and the rebellious devils will keep far from him, and he will be free of shirk, and his two guardian angels will testify for him on the Day of Resurrection that he was a believer in the messengers." [[Narrated by al-Tha'labi, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Wahidi by more than one route, from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, may God be pleased with him.]]
